references.text: Moses uses the same argument in his intercession after the golden calf incident, where he asks God to consider what the Egyptians would say if He destroyed the people – that the Lord brought them out with evil intentions to kill them in the mountains.
A similar concern is expressed here: if God destroys the people, the nations will say that the Lord was not able to bring them into the promised land, and therefore He killed them in the wilderness.
Joshua expresses a similar concern about what the Canaanites would say and do against God's name if Israel were destroyed.
Reference to the promise of the land that God spoke to the fathers, the same promise that Moses fears the nations will say God was unable to fulfill.
Moses argues that the Egyptians will hear about it and tell it further to the inhabitants of the land, which would dishonor God's name.
The Israelites themselves accused God of hating them and of having brought them out of Egypt to deliver them into the hands of the Amorites to be destroyed.
